## Diabetes Mellitus {.poster-slide}

::: {.poster-heading}
**How insulin, blood glucose, and health are connected**<br>
Example Student · BIOL 110 · The Community College of Baltimore County
:::

::: {.poster-lead}
**The central idea:** Diabetes mellitus is a group of conditions in which blood glucose stays too high because insulin is absent, insufficient, or not working effectively. [1, 2]
:::

:::: {.poster-grid}

::: {.poster-panel}
**Blood glucose regulation**

| After a meal | Between meals |
|:--|:--|
| Blood glucose rises → pancreatic beta cells release **insulin** → tissues take up or store more glucose; the liver reduces glucose release. | Blood glucose falls → the pancreas releases **glucagon** → the liver releases stored glucose. |

Diabetes disrupts this regulation through changes in insulin production, insulin action, or both. [1, 2]
:::

::: {.poster-panel}
**Three major types**

**Type 1** — An autoimmune process damages insulin-producing beta cells. Little or no insulin is made; insulin therapy is essential. [1, 2]

**Type 2** — Tissues become less responsive to insulin, and beta cells may not meet the body's needs. Multiple factors contribute. [1, 2]

**Gestational** — High blood glucose develops during pregnancy. Follow-up testing after birth matters because future type 2 risk is higher. [1, 2]
:::

::: {.poster-panel}
**Possible signs & diagnosis**

Possible signs include increased thirst or urination, hunger, fatigue, blurry vision, or unexplained weight loss. Some people have no noticeable symptoms. [2]

**Diabetes-range results for nonpregnant people** [1, 3]

| Test | Result |
|:--|:--|
| A1C | **≥ 6.5%** |
| Fasting plasma glucose | **≥ 126 mg/dL** |
| 2-hour glucose tolerance test | **≥ 200 mg/dL** |
| Random plasma glucose | **≥ 200 mg/dL** with classic symptoms or hyperglycemic crisis |

Without unequivocal hyperglycemia, an abnormal result is generally confirmed with repeat testing. Pregnancy uses different criteria. [1, 3]
:::

::: {.poster-panel}
**Protecting health**

Long-term high blood glucose can damage blood vessels and nerves, raising the risk of eye, kidney, nerve, and heart disease or stroke. Complications are not inevitable. [1, 2]

- **Type 1:** insulin is essential.
- **Type 2:** individualized nutrition, activity, medicines, and/or insulin.
- **All types:** monitoring and preventive checks with a health-care team. [4]
- Healthy habits or programs can lower type 2 risk, not eliminate it; type 1 has no established prevention. [2]
:::

::::
